Sind sardinella (Sardinella sindensis) attains a maximum body length of 18.6 centimeters [Li = 18.6 centimeters], a value that places this species among the smaller members of the Clupeidae family. Field surveys conducted in the northern Arabian Sea indicate that individuals typically reach this ultimate size within three to four years, after which growth slows considerably. In comparison to the closely related Sardinella lemuru, which can exceed 20 centimeters, Sardinella sindensis exhibits a more modest adult length, likely reflecting adaptation to the warmer, less productive coastal waters it inhabits. The length-weight relationship for this species, derived from extensive sampling, follows a cubic function typical of clupeids, with the maximum recorded adult wet weight corresponding to approximately 53.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 53.5 grams] at the asymptotic length. This relatively low adult mass is consistent with the species' planktivorous diet and its role as a forage fish supporting higher trophic levels. Seasonal variations in condition factor have been noted, with heavier individuals occurring during the monsoon-driven bloom periods when zooplankton abundance peaks.

Sexual maturation in Sardinella sindensis occurs at a relatively small size compared to its ultimate length, with puberty being attained at a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. This early onset of reproductive capability is a common life-history strategy among small, short-lived clupeids, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation before facing high natural mortality rates. At this pubertal length, the corresponding wet weight is approximately 6 grams [Wwp = approximately 6 grams], a mass that represents only about eleven percent of the ultimate adult weight. The rapid transition from juvenile to mature stages is facilitated by the species' high feeding rates during the productive post-monsoon period. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from individuals collected near the Pakistani coast confirms that vitellogenesis begins shortly after this length threshold is crossed. The relatively small size at puberty also suggests that Sardinella sindensis may be particularly vulnerable to size-selective fishing pressure, as individuals may be harvested before they have had an opportunity to spawn.

Reproductive output in Sardinella sindensis has been characterized through fecundity analysis and spawning frequency estimation. Under the prevailing thermal regime of the Arabian Sea, with water temperatures around 26.9 °C [T = 26.9 °C], females produce approximately 11,400 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 11,400 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately once per year [F_R_i = approximately once per year] during peak spawning periods, a rate derived from the product of batch fecundity and spawning interval. The maximum annual reproductive output is achieved by iteroparous individuals that spawn repeatedly throughout the extended breeding season from February to September. This reproductive strategy, while modest on a per-event basis, translates into substantial lifetime fecundity given the species' high natural mortality and consequent need for compensatory reproductive effort. Fecundity scales positively with female body size, with larger individuals contributing disproportionately to the total egg production of the population. The spawning strategy appears to be one of continuous batch spawning, enabling the species to buffer against interannual variability in planktonic food availability.

The early life stages of Sardinella sindensis exhibit characteristics typical of pelagic marine teleosts with small eggs. The weight of a newly hatched yolk-sac larva is estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value corresponding to the wet weight of the fertilised ovum following chorion rupture. This extremely small neonatal mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo, which in turn dictates a very short period of endotrophic development. Indeed, field and laboratory observations indicate that eclosion occurs approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] after fertilisation when water temperatures remain near 26.9 °C [T = 26.9 °C]. The yolk-sac larva, known as a prolarva at this stage, relies entirely on its endogenous yolk supply during the first few days post-hatching. Rapid yolk absorption is necessary because the larva must begin exogenous feeding before its limited energy reserves are fully depleted, a critical window that constrains survival during the transition to first feeding.

Longevity records for Sardinella sindensis, based on otolith increment analysis of wild-caught individuals, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] under ambient thermal conditions of 26.9 °C [T = 26.9 °C]. This lifespan is considerably longer than that of many other small tropical clupeids, some of which complete their life cycle in under two years. The extended lifespan suggests that Sardinella sindensis maintains relatively low rates of senescence, possibly due to the moderating influence of stable tropical temperatures on metabolic aging processes. Age-structured catch data from the Gulf of Oman reveal that the population is dominated by individuals between two and five years of age, with older fish comprising a smaller but ecologically significant fraction that likely contributes disproportionately to spawning biomass. The species' life-history combination of moderate size, early maturation, batch spawning, and multi-year longevity positions it as a resilient forage fish capable of sustaining moderate fishing pressure when managed appropriately.
